children: Warren Buffett (Trades, Portfolio) is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A) (BRK.B), closing another chapter in one of the most consequential leadership tenures in corporate history and putting the conglomerate's long-planned succession structure fully into place.
Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and remain on Berkshire's board.
His son Howard G. Buffett, who has served on the board for 33 years, will become chairman, while Susan Decker stays on as lead independent director.
The move comes less than a year after Greg Abel became CEO, succeeding Buffett after roughly six decades in the role.

"Father Time always wins," Buffett told shareholders. "He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead."
Buffett also gave Abel a powerful endorsement.

"My expectations for him were sky high from the start, and he has exceeded them," Buffett said. "He has taken hold of the chief executive officer job in every respect. He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them."
Berkshire shares slipped about 0.1% in Friday premarket trading.

Buffett took control of Berkshire in 1965 and transformed what had been a struggling textile company into a diversified conglomerate spanning insurance, railroads, energy, aerospace components, retail, real estate, truck stops and homebuilding.
Berkshire also manages an equity portfolio worth nearly $300 billion, with major holdings including Alphabet (GOOGL), Apple

Abel already controls day-to-day operating decisions, while Howard Buffett's chairman role appears designed to protect Berkshire's culture rather than recreate Warren Buffett (Trades, Portfolio)'s investment role.
That distinction matters because Berkshire's future will increasingly depend on institutional processes rather than one individual.
Investors should watch capital allocation under Abel, acquisition discipline and whether Berkshire's decentralized operating model remains intact.

Buffett's continued board presence should soften the transition, but the market is now entering a period where Berkshire must prove its competitive advantages can endure without Buffett formally at the top.

title: Berkshire's Next Chapter Comes With a Buffett-Sized Question
